Guides

A week, in outline

These are examples, not rules. Swap in whichever iron food and allergen you’re working on.

Key points

At six months, portions are small and milk feeds carry on. One or two meals a day, each with an iron-rich food, is plenty to begin with.
At nine months, the focus is texture and keeping allergens regular. Three meals, soft finger foods, and peanut or egg on several days.
At twelve months, your child eats family food, with their portion unsalted. Milk becomes a drink from a cup, in moderate amounts.

Around six months

Breakfast could be oat porridge with cooked apple, with a teaspoon of smooth peanut butter stirred in once peanut has been tried. Lunch could be chicken, sweet potato, and broccoli, mashed. If your baby wants a second meal, try red lentil soup or egg mashed into vegetables.

Over the week, deliberately repeat egg, peanut, wheat, and a dairy food. Keep breast milk or formula as the main drink. Offer water, but don’t push it.

Around nine months

Breakfast: porridge or egg with fruit. Lunch: soft pasta with tomato and mince, or fish with rice and greens. Afternoon snack: yogurt or a soft vegetable fritter. Dinner can be the family’s stew, mashed, taken out before the salt goes in.

Finger foods go alongside the spoon: a strip of soft cooked pepper, a piece of ripe pear, a flake of salmon. If you haven’t already, this is the age to leave thin purée behind.

Around twelve months

Meals now look like everyone else’s. Bread and fruit for breakfast, a bean stew or pasta for lunch, baked egg or leftover meat in the evening. Snacks are fruit, yogurt, or a soft oat bite, not a sweet biscuit out of habit.

Honey is now considered safer as far as botulism goes, but it’s still a poor everyday sweetener. Keep halving grapes lengthways. Whole nuts are still years away. A little salt can go into family food; your child’s portion doesn’t need as much as an adult’s.
